title: What inspired means
hookLine: all-scripture-is-God-breathed (2 Timothy 3:16) is read by some as word-for-word, by others as God working through human writers

cards: Dust, shaped into a person, lying still on the ground. Not alive yet. Then, in the second chapter of Genesis, God leans close: "and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul."

Dust, plus breath, equals someone. Hold that picture, because a short line in a letter that opens with Paul's name reaches for the same breath, and Christians read it in more than one way. Today's word: inspiration.

teach.b: The word inspiration carries a picture of breath.
The line is in the second letter to Timothy: "All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness."
Behind the King James phrase is a Greek word, theopneustos, usually rendered God-breathed. Genesis again: God breathes, and something lifeless comes alive. Notice what the verse spends its breath on.

It doesn't explain how the breathing worked. It says what scripture is for: teaching, correcting, setting straight, training. It's written to Timothy, who, it says, has known the holy scriptures from a child.
It's practical. The how is where Christians read differently.
Some, often evangelical, stress that God guided the writers so closely that the very words are what God intended, and teach that the Bible is without error in all it affirms.

teach.h: WORD FOR WORD, OR THROUGH WRITERS?
teach.b: Others put the weight on God working through human writers: their languages, styles, times and personalities.

Catholic teaching holds the two together: God is the author of scripture, the human writers are true authors too, and the books teach without error the truth God wanted written down for our salvation.
Orthodox and Protestant teachers stand at different points along that line.

Both sides lean on a verse in the second letter of Peter: "holy men of God spake as they were moved by the Holy Ghost." Divine and human in the same sentence. Christians argue about how much weight each half carries.
They agree on the breath: a book that, they say, didn't just get written. It got breathed into.

how: Christians call the Bible inspired, God-breathed; some, often evangelical, stress that its very words are without error, others stress God working through true human authors, and Catholic teaching affirms both.

games.q: you're Timothy, reading a letter that says all scripture is God-breathed. what does it say scripture is for?
o: for settling exactly how God breathed it.
for doctrine, reproof, correction and instruction in righteousness.
games.why: the verse spends its breath on use, not mechanics: teaching, correcting, setting straight, training. the how is where Christians read it differently.

practice: Breathe in, and on the out-breath say quietly: all scripture is given by inspiration of God. On the next out-breath: and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, for instruction in righteousness.
Then just breathe, noticing that every word rode out on air; if you pray, ask that the words you read be alive for you, and if not, simply rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Inspiration. A breath word. In 2 Timothy, scripture is God-breathed, and useful for teaching and training.

carryVoice: Your line: god-breathed. Dust, and then breath, and then someone comes alive. See you tomorrow.
